Turbine can simulate any algorithmically definable dynamics on very large networks (up to millions of nodes and edges) on a standard desktop computer.
The 'communicating vessels' model used in Turbine gives an exponential decay of perturbations, in agreement with previous findings.

Benchmark networks with pronounced modular structure (5% inter-modular edges) had a 4.8 times larger 'fill time' (time to affect 80% of nodes) compared to networks with fuzzy modular structure (40% inter-modular edges).

Perturbation centrality is defined as the reciprocal of 'silencing time' - the first time step when all nodes have an energy value less than 1 after an initial perturbation of 10*n units (n = number of nodes).
Perturbation centrality had the highest correlation with closeness centrality (0.67 on average), followed by community centrality (0.65) and weighted degree (0.69).
In benchmark networks, inter-modular non-hub nodes had 87% higher perturbation centrality than intra-modular hubs in networks with pronounced modular structure.

The top 100 perturbation centrality nodes in the unstressed yeast interactome had only 42 nodes in common with the top 100 in the heat-shocked interactome, but 65 and 68 nodes in common with the oxidatively- and osmotically-stressed interactomes, respectively.
Perturbation centrality successfully identified the active site and substrate binding sites of the Met-tRNA synthetase protein as the regions with the largest increase upon substrate binding.
